topic: Everyone blames winter for a dead battery. Summer already did the damage.
mechanicTruth: Heat, not cold, is the primary driver of battery failure: elevated under-hood temperature accelerates the internal chemical reaction, corrodes the plates faster, and evaporates electrolyte fluid over the course of a hot season. The failure is usually only noticed on the first cold morning, when a weakened battery can no longer deliver enough cold-cranking amps — but the damage accumulated all summer, not that morning.
driverConfusion: Drivers associate a dead battery with cold weather because that's when the no-start actually happens, so they check/replace batteries heading into winter and never think about a Cleveland summer as the risk window.
clevelandAngle: Cleveland runs both halves of this myth for real: humid 80-90F summer stretches cook a battery under the hood, then the area's sharp autumn cold snap is exactly when the weakened battery finally fails to crank. REEL-SLATE-2026-07-31.md item #12 already carries the brand-voice-approved line 'Most batteries last three to five years. Cleveland winters are hard on them' — this pack extends that with the heat mechanism, it does not contradict it.

selectedCaption:
Everyone blames the first cold morning. The real damage happened all summer.

Heat speeds up the chemical reaction inside a battery — it corrodes the plates and evaporates the fluid, quietly, all season, under a hot engine hood. The cold morning is just when it finally shows.

Most batteries last three to five years, and Cleveland heat shortens that. If yours is close, come by for a free check before the first cold snap.

17625 Euclid Ave, Cleveland OH · (216) 862-0005
